manual.purpose: The control plane every tool (portal, CLI, Terraform) talks to.
facts: Every create, update or delete goes through ARM, whichever tool you use. You don't enable it; it is part of the platform.
ARM checks RBAC on every request and evaluates Azure Policy when one is assigned. Role and policy assignments are themselves ARM resources.
Resource providers (Microsoft.Compute, Microsoft.Network, ...) must be registered per subscription before you can create that type of resource.
Terraform's azurerm provider calls ARM's REST API resource by resource and keeps its own state file. It does not generate ARM templates.
Bicep is an Azure-only language that compiles to an ARM template (JSON), which ARM's deployment engine applies. No state file: Azure itself is the record. Preview changes with what-if.

Both describe desired state, but a deployment is one-shot: nothing keeps reconciling afterward (unlike a Kubernetes controller). Drift is found by re-running plan or what-if, or corrected by Azure Policy effects such as DeployIfNotExists.

manual.purpose: Grant a role to an identity at a given scope.
facts: Three parts: who (principal), what (role), where (scope). Scopes inherit downward.
Contributor manages resources but is not a data role. Use data roles such as Key Vault Secrets User for secrets.
RBAC answers 'who may do what?'. Azure Policy answers 'what is allowed to exist, and how must it be configured?'. Full access does not bypass policy.
A role assignment is its own ARM resource, stored at a scope, so one group assignment can cover many resources. That is why RBAC scales better than per-resource lists.

manual.purpose: Secretless identities for Azure resources, rotated by Azure.

No stored secret; short-lived tokens come from the platform.
Useless until it has a role assignment.

review.note: Imported from the first hand-drafted page; not yet checked against Microsoft Learn.

manual.purpose: Store secrets, keys and certificates with access control.
facts: Prefer RBAC with a data role such as Key Vault Secrets User for reading secrets.
Contributor is a management role, not a secrets role.
Permission model: either vault access policies or Azure RBAC, one at a time. Access policies are a property stored inside the vault, not a separate service.
Switching to RBAC ignores existing access policies, so create the equivalent role assignments first and test before switching.

manual.purpose: Enforce and audit rules on resources.
facts: Rules about resource configuration, not about who may act. Examples: allowed regions, required tags, no public IPs, storage must disable public access.
Assigned at a management group, subscription or resource group and inherited downward; specific scopes can be excluded. It only applies to the resource types and properties its rule matches.
Effects: Deny, Audit, Modify, Append, DeployIfNotExists, AuditIfNotExists, Disabled. Evaluated on create and update, plus a periodic compliance scan. Existing resources are not deleted.
If a Terraform apply fails with RequestDisallowedByPolicy, read the policy name in the error before debugging the code.
